title: Pattern-Making Station
strapline: Red, blue, red, blue — and the thrilling question of what comes next.
intent: Children copy, continue and create repeating patterns — the root of mathematical thinking is spotting and using regularity.
Children learn to predict: once you see the rule, you know what comes next, and being right feels wonderful.
Children build the vocabulary of pattern — repeat, next, again, the same, different — through handling beautiful materials.
Children move from simple ABAB patterns towards more complex ones (ABB, ABC) at their own pace.
Children see pattern everywhere once they're tuned to it — in music, movement, the day's routine, the natural world.
implementation: Stock a low table with sortable loose parts in strong colours and shapes — pebbles, buttons, gems, bottle-tops, pegs.
Start a pattern and leave it deliberately unfinished where a child will find it and feel the pull to continue.
Model the rule out loud, pointing along: 'red, blue, red, blue — so what do you think comes next?'
Make a mistake in your own pattern for children to catch and put right — spotting the break is real understanding.
Offer pattern strips and a peg loom so patterns can be copied and displayed, then invented from scratch.
Widen the idea beyond colour: clap-stamp-clap-stamp, or a pattern of big-small-big-small objects.
Photograph and name each child's pattern — 'Ava's ABB pattern' — so the maths language becomes theirs.
key_questions: What comes next in your pattern? How do you know?
Can you tell me the rule you're using?
I think I made a mistake — can you spot where my pattern went wrong?
Could you make the same pattern a different way?
Where else can you see a pattern in the room?

impact.text: Children copy and continue a simple repeating pattern.
Children create their own patterns and explain the rule.
Children spot and fix a mistake in a pattern.
Children use pattern language — repeat, next, same, different.
Children notice patterns in the wider world and point them out.
Children stay with a long pattern until it's complete.

enhancements: A peg loom or threading strips so patterns can be built and kept.
Natural pattern-making outdoors: leaves, sticks, stones and shells on a tray.
Pattern cards to copy, then challenge cards with the last item hidden.
A sound-and-movement pattern basket: shakers, claves and scarves for clap-stamp patterns.
A mirror or symmetry board to explore reflected patterns.
Printed patterned fabrics, wrapping paper and tiles to hunt for repeats.

playing_exploring: Beautiful, sortable materials invite children to arrange and rearrange freely.
Children set their own pattern puzzles for others to continue.
active_learning: Completing a long pattern exactly gives a satisfaction children return to.
Children persist to fix a pattern that has gone wrong.
creating_thinking: Children spot the rule and use it to predict what comes next.
They invent new and more complex patterns, holding the rule in mind.
